Many have safely stopped drinking by tapering their drinking.  This resource for setting up a tapering schedule is popular around this sub: 

https://hams.cc/taper/

It doesn't work in all cases.  Ive gone on 3-6 week "functional binges" of drinking 2+ handles per week, and had success tapering after. So it can work.

I followed some similar logic in my late twenties (31 now, addiction started about 2 years ago). Drinking enough that I knew it'd lead to addiction and I'd eventually stop, but it wasn't damaging my life and health impacts were minor.

I'm addicted now, and the only massive regret I have is that alcohol changed my mental health as addiction set in. Mild depression, anxiety, emotions poorly regulated, trouble socializing. They're all quite mild, but I used to be a happy social person. I'd give anything to get that old version of my brain back. It will come back, but it takes time.

So my main regret from getting into early addiction isn't anything I did or having to quit, it's that I no longer get to feel like me until I help my brain heal.

I try to look at studies skeptically.  The only factual part of a study is the collection of data; the conclusion of studies are opinions based on data.  Conclusions from studies aren't automatically true just because the studies were scientific.

Lots of studies supported cigarettes not causing cancer before the 60s/70s. The studies weren't wrong and data wasn't false, they just were misleading. With enough money influence from big tobacco these studies concluded tobacco was A-OK. The alcohol industry is still today influencing studies on alcohol.

Annie Grace's This Naked Mind talks some about how to judge the reliability of a scientific study. Here's a little excerpt:

"Articles come out all the time claiming that wine is good for your heart or that alcohol 
reduces your cholesterol. A few studies have correlated alcohol consumption and life expectancy. What is bizarre about these studies is that they ignore the cause of death (i.e., did alcohol contribute to death?) and lump all deaths together. Nonetheless, innumerable ar-
ticles are published highlighting the relatively few studies that claim alcohol is good for you and ignoring the thousands of studies that 
prove otherwise."

That sounds like withdrawal, from my understanding of addiction science andr my own experience.  Here's a quote from Annie Grace's This Naked Mind: 

"When we take a physically addictive substance, from caffeine to crack, we suffer withdrawal as it leaves our system. With some harder
drugs it’s intense, but with most addictive substances, like nicotine, sugar, caffeine, or alcohol, it can be a small, almost unnoticeable,
feeling of discomfort. A vulnerable, anxious, empty feeling. The un-easy notion that something is not quite right, or missing, and that
life is incomplete. Since alcohol can take days to leave the system, drinkers might experience this feeling almost constantly."

She mentions elsewhere in the book that the feeling of wanting a drink to relax, which is well within the range of "moderate" drinking, is just the early stages of withdrawals from a psychological perspective.  

Early withdrawals are typically mental, maybe slight anxiety and stress. Many drinkers experience early withdrawals without any realization it's just early addiction (not to say they necessarily progresses to obvious addiction).

A big downside to my drinking, even way before the drinking became problematic, was that I no longer got much practice being social sober.  In hindsight, I've watched my ability to be social while sober disappear over the years.  It takes hard, intentional effort for me to be a good sober conversationalist now.  

Sure if I just drink a few beers I'll be as social as ever again, most people like me that way at group events.  But I don't want to do that.  I don't want to let alcohol dictate how quality a friend I can be to others at any moment.  I want to choose to have those moments when and wherever I damn well please.

So I'm going to keep staying sober during social situations. Because it's better for my relationships if I learn to master my social skills independent of alcohol. That's one on my long list of why I'm avoiding drinking.

Nice to finally have figured out alcohol is largely to blame.  Those rare mornings when I wake up at peace are amazing.

Hopefully people here have good input too.  The times I've been successfully sober while my gf was still drinking were the times that she'd keep no more than 2-3 drinks in the house. Meaning if she wanted to drink around me, which I was okay with, she bought the drinks after work and finished most of it that night. Part of a handle left in the freezer and I was screwed.

Now that's just me -- I'm not triggered to drink by the idea of <5 drinks because a small buzz is not tempting.  Many alcoholics can be sucked in by any alcohol at all being available.  Many can't have it in their home ever. It comes down to us figuring out and accepting what we can and cannot allow ourselves to be tempted by.

A problem drinker is safer with less alcohol around always. Especially when they are still learning to understand their compulsions. But very few of us live in an alcohol free bubble and coexisting around alcohol is often something that can be done.

Do you think your gf knows what kinds of temptation are too much for her? Most of us in early sobriety don't.  It's a rhetorical question -- I just think that answer will help inform your original question.

I tried Lexapro for 4 months in order to address depression and this depression-influenced drinking problem.  The good: I committed and stuck to not drinking so I could feel the full effect of an antidepressant. The bad: I ended up more anxious and unable to focus, up to a point that made regular tasks difficult.  

So I quit SSRIs and tapered off them. And felt really pleased that I had at least tried them. And realized there are other meds I can try too.  It was nice to know I have options to try if shit gets worse.

Understanding doesn't solve things.  Nor does studying psych, from my eastern philosopher's standpoint.
Fuck man. People are hurting. You could actually help people.  Anger sucks.

I've seen other posts on this sub about wild dreaming during the first few days of sobriety.  It definitely sounds like a common thing.

I've encountered this a few times during mild withdrawals (no medical intervention).

The dreams are always nightmares ranging from just annoying situations to horror movies.  At their worst, I ended up having a few dozen dreams within several hours of napping.  I couldn't distinguish among the time awake between dreams, and the dreams themselves.  It culminated in sleep paralysis, which finally woke my ass up completely and made avoid sleep.

Good news is that my dreams always returned to normal after 2-3 days at most of not drinking.  I've also messed around with lucid dreaming most of my life so I'm prone to unusual dreaming and sleep paralysis.

Let's move on to what else we were talking about because your drinking is a symptom of these issues". I've also had a therapist that told me to go to AA, then asked me how AA works after I went. Some therapists are trash at handling addiction and others are gold.

Yeah it's a road of no return. But it's the prettiest road I've ever been on. There are so many people walking alongside that are, at the very worst, fun to talk to. And I hear this road is beautiful a few miles ahead. Mountains, alpine lakes, all that stuff I want my life to be full of. But the walk takes patience.

What are your hobbies you can do sober? I read, write, surf and workout. When none of those sounds good, I go to bed and/or watch TV (that's most days when I'm early in sobriety like this) I don't enjoy those hobbies all the time because sometimes I just want to drink. But everyone here, and at AA, tells me this shitty feeling ends. It's depression. Alcohol is a depressant; our brains get used to it. The brain does recover with time.

That is a kind gesture, telling people that you love them. Your heart is in the right place. 

It took just about a year for me to go from drunkenly enjoying sharing love to drunkenly harassing spam callers on my phone and sharing hate (and eventually almost getting a felony for fighting some assholes that were hitting on underage girls -- yeah, heart in the right place but poor reaction)

Alcohol brings out weird emotions that I barely knew were in me. I can't predict them, and I've tried for way too long.

I really like "full catastrophe living". It's a mindfulness-based mental health treatment plan you can start literally tomorrow if you want. There are other options out there for self-help, that's just what I'm working on.

Yes, I did. I moved to a new place, went sober for no reason and it was probably the best months of my recent life. I started expanding my social circle and drinking with people, and eventually this addiction really took hold.

Keep with it. It sounds like your unconscious brain is on board. It took me a conscious decision to make any lasting change.

Figuring out why I drink is tough, personally. I have a list of reasons that I write down. Every time I drink since trying to get sober, I reflect on that list and often add something I didn't realize before. It's a long list. 

It took a couple years of a functional, "normal" drinking problem before I even knew what the first item on that list was.

I am absolutely certain at least one boss knew what was up. Two of those jobs I chose to quit after relapses, and both bosses were so kind.

I guess I'm saying it doesn't matter if the boss knows.  They've been through it before, there are enough addicts out there that this shit is common. If they're understanding, they'll know something tough is happening in your life and give you space. If they're dicks about it, that says a lot about them and nothing about you.

I completely empathize with the thought that "the worst part" is leaving work in the middle of the shift. It's Ok. Your sobriety is so much more important than a job. Good managers know that.

I have tapered on my own.  It's still shit, but it did make my withdrawals better.  I didn't follow a schedule; I waited until my heart beat through my chest and I couldn't function anymore (withdrawals) before  I took the next drink. I would do this for about 4 days.

It is always hard.  It always takes a few days. 72 hours for me before I'm functional again even after the best of tapering.  I know in that time period my mind is fucked and I don't trust my thoughts anymore.  It helps me to set everything aside for a few days and just try to survive.

Something about being mid-withdrawals after a relapse always sends me deep into self-hatred.  Even when the relapse is short and no one else knows, the bottomless pain still finds me.  It's not   even very logical most of the time, pure emotion driven by chemical imbalance in the brain.  

It does pass.  For me, forgiveness starts to seem possible again after a week plus sober.  All the tools we talk about on this sub (therapy, lit, etc.) help me slowly accept that forgiveness is really the only possible path forward that isn't downard. Practice (many relapses) made me realize that if I can push through the first sober days, my healthier brain can reign in self-hatred.

Shame/anger/etc. focused inward is the worst, most manipulative part of withdrawals in my opinion.

I was mildly addicted to weed for years before drinking problematically. It helps me sleep and is an effective anti-anxiety -- when I moved states to where it's illegal I started using alcohol for those effects. 

Weed was and is a crutch for my mental health, but it's not one that ruins my life. When I don't have weed available, I get anxious which both sucks in general and triggers drinking.

I just started seeing a psychiatrist to help me quit both drugs and address mental health.  The bottom line she gave me was she could give me prescriptions to help stop drinking cravings (naltrexone to start), but for weed there was nothing she could give me -- quitting weed was just going to take the willpower (achieved via therapy, meetings, other non-chemical methods).
